ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure shows a rectangular room with a grid, with a thick black boundary wall at the top; in the upper left there is an opening labeled G, about 3 grid cells wide. On the right, black arrows pointing left-right and up-down are drawn, indicating that these shapes can only translate horizontally or vertically and cannot rotate. Inside the room there are five black polyomino shapes A, B, C, D, and E; C has an obvious long horizontal bar, the lower part of E has a relatively large horizontal span, A and D are bent shapes with protruding blocks, and B is located toward the upper right and has a relatively compact staggered shape. Reasoning: According to the problem, treat each shape as a fixed combination of grid cells, which can only translate through the 3-cell-wide door G at the top. When leaving, any row of cells currently passing through the top wall line must lie completely within the range of the 3 door columns of G. C has a horizontal row with width greater than 3 cells, so it cannot pass through. E’s horizontal outline/span also exceeds 3 cells, so it cannot pass through. Although the local row widths of A and D do not necessarily all exceed the door width, their upper and lower protruding parts require different horizontal alignments; when one part is aligned with the 3-cell door, another part will extend under the wall outside the door, so they cannot get out by translation alone. B’s staggered outline can be aligned row by row with this 3-cell door, and during upward movement it can keep the cells that are passing through the wall inside the door through small horizontal adjustments, so it can leave. Conclusion: The shape that can leave through G is B.

method.method_draft: Manual doorway-profile test. First describe the image: there is a rectangular grid room with a horizontal top wall, a three-grid-square opening labeled G near the upper left, and five black polyomino-like figures labeled A–E inside; the side arrows show that pieces may translate left, right, up, and down, but not rotate. Read from the text that the task is to identify which one can leave through G. Treat each figure as a fixed set of occupied grid squares. For each figure, compare its row-by-row horizontal profile with the three-square gate while imagining it sliding upward through the top wall. A legal passage requires every set of squares that crosses the wall at any instant to fit inside the gate columns, with only left/right/up/down shifts allowed between steps. Figures C and E have a row or horizontal span that is too wide for the gate; A and D have overhanging row arrangements that force incompatible horizontal alignments while crossing. Figure B has the only staggered profile that can be aligned with the gate and wiggled upward through it without rotation. Conclude that B can leave through gate G.

ready3_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure shows a rectangular room with a grid, with a thick black boundary wall at the top; in the upper left there is an opening labeled G, about 3 grid cells wide. On the right, black arrows pointing left-right and up-down are drawn, indicating that these shapes can only translate horizontally or vertically and cannot rotate. Inside the room there are five black polyomino shapes A, B, C, D, and E; C has an obvious long horizontal bar, the lower part of E has a relatively large horizontal span, A and D are bent shapes with protruding blocks, and B is located toward the upper right and has a relatively compact staggered shape. Reasoning: According to the problem, treat each shape as a fixed combination of grid cells, which can only translate through the 3-cell-wide door G at the top. When leaving, any row of cells currently passing through the top wall line must lie completely within the range of the 3 door columns of G. C has a horizontal row with width greater than 3 cells, so it cannot pass through. E’s horizontal outline/span also exceeds 3 cells, so it cannot pass through. Although the local row widths of A and D do not necessarily all exceed the door width, their upper and lower protruding parts require different horizontal alignments; when one part is aligned with the 3-cell door, another part will extend under the wall outside the door, so they cannot get out by translation alone. B’s staggered outline can be aligned row by row with this 3-cell door, and during upward movement it can keep the cells that are passing through the wall inside the door through small horizontal adjustments, so it can leave. Conclusion: The shape that can leave through G is B.
